issues.legal_issue: An accused relying on private defence must establish a factual basis for that defence on a preponderance of probabilities, but need not prove it beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The accused claimed that the deceased fired at him and that he returned fire in self-defence, and also claimed that the deceased was stealing paddy from a field in which the accused had a property interest.
Medical expert evidence supported the finding that the accused’s injuries were not caused by gunshots in the manner he claimed and had been fabricated to create a defence.

The accused did not produce the alleged nearby witnesses or elicit evidence from prosecution witnesses establishing that the deceased fired at him, stole or attempted to steal paddy, or that the accused was entitled to the paddy.
Prosecution witnesses denied that the deceased fired a weapon or that the deceased and another person stole paddy.
issues.conclusion: The accused did not discharge the burden of establishing a factual basis for private defence of either person or property.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, but the accused’s burden to establish private defence is less onerous and may be discharged by showing a mere preponderance of probabilities, either through cross-examination of prosecution witnesses or by adducing defence evidence. The accused need not establish the plea to the hilt. The Court relied on Partap v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1976 SC 966, and Munshi Ram & Ors. v. Delhi Administration, [1968] 2 SCR 455.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding is a criminal case in which the accused’s criminal liability is being determined.
predicates.accused_claimed_private_defence: The accused asserted that the force used was justified to defend a person or property.
predicates.defence_basis_established_on_preponderan: The accused produced or elicited evidence making it more probable than not that circumstances justifying private defence existed.
predicates.private_defence_not_established: The accused’s claim of private defence is not accepted as established.

issues.definition: In a criminal case, when the accused claims private defence but does not make its factual basis more probable than not through defence evidence or cross-examination, the claim is not established.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court hearing an appeal against acquittal may review the evidence and reverse the acquittal, while giving proper consideration to the trial judge’s credibility findings, the presumption of innocence, reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after accepting his account that he had fired in private defence, although it considered the prosecution account to be true.
The High Court reviewed the evidence, rejected the accused’s account, and relied on prosecution witnesses whose account the trial court itself regarded as truthful.
The evidence supported the finding that the accused fired at the deceased without justifiable provocation, and the asserted private-defence account was not established.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had not overlooked the principles governing appeals against acquittal and was justified in reversing an acquittal based on surmises and conjectures.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reversing the acquittal and convicting the accused; the Supreme Court upheld that reversal and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: In an appeal against acquittal under section 417 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, the appellate court has full power to review the evidence and reach its own conclusion. Expressions such as “substantial and compelling reasons” do not limit that power, but the appellate court must properly consider the trial judge’s view of witness credibility, the presumption of innocence, the accused’s entitlement to the benefit of any real and reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s advantage in seeing witnesses. The Court relied on Sheo Swarup v. King Emperor, 61 I.A. 398; Nur Mohammad v. Emperor, AIR 1945 PC 151; Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan, [1961] 3 SCR 120; Ramaphupala Reddy & Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, [1970] 3 SCC 474; Gopi Nath Ganga Ram Surve & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra, [1970] 3 SCC 627; Dharam Das & Ors. v. State of U.P., [1973] 2 SCC 216; Lekha Yadav v. State of Bihar, [1973] 2 SCC 424; Samson Hyam Kemkar v. State of Maharashtra, [1974] 3 SCC 494; and Barati v. State of U.P., [1974] 4 SCC 258.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of an acquittal.
predicates.prosecution_case_supported_by_credible_e: The prosecution evidence supports the alleged offence and is regarded as credible, including by the trial court where applicable.
predicates.trial_acquittal_based_on_speculation: The acquittal rests on conjecture rather than a sound assessment of the evidence.
predicates.appellate_court_considered_acquittal_saf: The appellate court gives proper consideration to the trial judge’s credibility findings, the presumption of innocence, reasonable doubt, and the trial judge’s opportunity to see the witnesses.
predicates.reversal_of_acquittal_justified: The appellate court’s reversal of the acquittal is justified.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, credible evidence supports the prosecution, the acquittal rests on speculation, and the appellate court considers the safeguards applicable to such appeals, reversal of the acquittal is justified.
